newsitem.title: USA: Intel profits rise 58 percent in second quarter.
newsitem.headline: Intel profits rise 58 percent in second quarter.

text.p: Intel Corp. on Tuesday reported a 58 percent rise in second-quarter profits, capping a challenging period for the semiconductor giant as it tries to make the transition to new, faster computer chips.

The world's largest maker of microprocessors earned $1.6 billion, or 92 cents a share, in the three months ended in June, slightly ahead of Wall Street's muted expectations for a profit of 90 cents a share.
However, Intel said third-quarter revenues would show little to no improvement from the second quarter, reflecting the continued shift toward Pentium MMX and Pentium II chips.

"Strong microprocessor shipments in the first quarter led to some inventory correction in the second quarter as the industry prepared for a rapid transition to processors with MMX (multimedia) technology," Intel Chairman Andrew Grove said. "Demand for the Pentium processor with MMX technology and the Pentium II processor is strong, and we are ramping production at a record rate."
Intel's results compared with a profit of $1.0 billion, or 59 cents a share, a year ago as revenues surged 29 percent to $6.0 billion from $4.6 billion in 1996's second quarter.

For the third quarter, Intel expects revenues to be flat to only slightly higher than the second quarter, suggesting the company's sequential growth will not be as robust as last year when third quarter revenues rose 11 percent.
The forecast is likely to prompt analysts to trim their third-quarter earnings estimates to below what Intel reported in the second quarter

"From the positive side, Intel's manufacturing is delivering," said Robert Chaplinsky, an analyst at investment bank Hambrecht & Quist. "The question is the transitioning -- the general health in near-term demand is really going to drive how fast they can get rid of mature Pentium (chips)."
Intel had prepared investors for a less-than-spectacular quarter when it warned more than a month ago that a slowdown in Europe would hurt revenues and earnings.
Nevertheless, Intel stock jumped more than $2 in after-hours trading to $83 because the numbers were not as bad as some market watchers had feared. Earlier, Intel closed at $80.91, up $2.16.
"It doesn't look bad," said C.B. Lee, an analyst at investment bank Sutro & Co., noting some analysts had warned Intel's second-quarter results could miss the Wall Street consensus figure.

Intel said gross margins -- the difference between sales and production costs -- are likely to be flat to slightly higher than the 61 percent reported in the second quarter. For the full year, Intel expects gross margins to remain around 60 percent, give or take a few percentage points.

Intel said the number of microprocessors and chipsets sold in the second quarter fell from the first quarter of 1997 and the number of motherboard units shipped in the second quarter was down from the first quarter of 1997. Motherboards are the main circuit board of a computer where the microprocessor chip sits.

Intel said motherboard units for the Pentium II processor were higher and flash memory shipments set a new record for the quarter. Flash memory is a small data storage card used in portable computing devices.
Intel bought back a total of 13 million shares in the quarter at a cost of $945 million.
Intel Chief Financial Officer Andy Bryant said in an interview the company has continued to buy back shares as part of a continuing programme.
"It's a bargain," he said of the practice of buying back Intel shares. "We believe a good use of the cash is to buy back our own stock. We think it's a pretty good investment."

Intel's earnings follow statements of weaker-than-expected June quarter results from chip makers Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Cyrix Corp., who are beginning to give Intel fresh competition for the first time in several years.
Like Intel, those companies are also dealing with a rapid shift to newer-generation microprocessors and feeling pricing pressures on older computer chips now being phased out.
